lesson_title: The Man Who Predicted Missing Elements
hook_text: In 1869 a chemist left holes in his chart and said: elements nobody has found yet go here. He was right.
clip_script: Dmitri Mendeleev wrote every known element on a card, sixty-three of them, and laid them out in order of mass. Whenever the behaviour started repeating, he began a new row, so families like lithium, sodium and potassium lined up in columns. But some spots did not fit. Instead of forcing them, he left gaps and described the elements that would one day fill them. Six years later, gallium was discovered, and it matched his prediction. Then scandium. Then germanium. That chart became the Periodic Table. Today it holds one hundred and eighteen elements, and it has a simple map: metals on the left, non-metals on the right, and semi-metals like silicon, the stuff in computer chips, on a zigzag staircase in between.
visual_style: Whiteboard cards being laid into a grid with three glowing question marks; the question marks flipping into Ga, Sc and Ge; then a coloured table with a zigzag staircase.
mood: Detective story with a triumphant reveal.
pacing: Mysterious build-up, three quick discoveries, a clear map at the end.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn to read the map of the elements.
